paper_metadata.title: LLM4Schema.org: Generating Schema.org Markups With Large Language Models
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper introduces LLM4Schema.org, an approach for evaluating large language models in generating Schema.org markups from webpage text. It reports that 40–50% of markup produced by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 is invalid, non-factual, or non-compliant with the Schema.org ontology, and that specialized LLM-powered agents can identify and remove these errors. After curation, GPT-4 outperforms human annotators in generating accurate and comprehensive Schema.org markups, while both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 improve areas where human annotators fall short.

paper_metadata-authors-01-01.excerpt: Minh-Hoang Dang, Thi Hoang Thi Pham, Pascal Molli, Hala Skaf-Molli and Alban Gaignard

paper_metadata-abstract-03-01.excerpt: Our study identifies that 40-50% of the markup produced by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are either invalid, non-factual, or non-compliant with the Schema.org ontology. We show that these errors can be identified and removed using specialized agents powered by LLMs. Once errors are filtered out, GPT-4 outperforms human annotators.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses how to generate reliable and sufficiently complete Schema.org JSON-LD markups from real, potentially lengthy webpage text when no complete ground-truth markup exists. It specifically investigates whether LLM-generated markup can outperform human-generated markup after filtering syntactic invalidity, unsupported statements, and violations of Schema.org property expectations.

methodology.description: LLM4Schema.org first extracts webpage body text and selects a target Schema.org type. An LLM is prompted with the target type, its allowed properties, Schema.org documentation examples, and the webpage content to generate JSON-LD. Long text is split into overlapping chunks and the outputs are merged. A custom SHACL-based Validity agent removes syntactically invalid types, properties, and values. An LLM-based Factuality agent checks each property-value-type triple against the webpage text, while an LLM-based Compliance agent checks each property value against the Schema.org property definition. The curated human and LLM markups are compared using the MIMR metric.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: Uses the Schema.org ontology as the target schema, including its types, properties, inheritance relationships, expected value types, and natural-language property definitions. The paper reports 806 types and 1476 properties. Generated JSON-LD is constrained and validated against Schema.org-derived SHACL shapes; compliance is checked against Schema.org documentation.

input_output.input_type: Rendered webpage HTML and its visible body text, together with a selected Schema.org target type; the evaluation also uses existing human-authored JSON-LD markup from the webpage.
input_output.input_granularity: Real-world complete webpages, processed as body text and divided into overlapping token chunks; the evaluation uses one selected target type and the corresponding root markup entity per webpage.
input_output.output_representation: Schema.org JSON-LD markup representing entities, typed properties, property values, nested entities, and RDF triples; curated output retains only valid, factual, and Schema.org-compliant property-value-type statements.

180 sampled webpages from six independent low/medium/high quantile groups
Schema.org documentation factuality ground truth: 785 positive, 498 intrinsic-negative, and 630 extrinsic-negative examples
Schema.org documentation compliance ground truth: 785 positive and 147 negative examples

baselines: Human-generated Schema.org markup from the webpages
evaluation.setting: The study evaluates three components: Factuality and Compliance agents on positive/negative tests derived from Schema.org documentation; and the complete pipeline on 180 real webpages sampled from WebDataCommons. Human and LLM markups receive the same validity, factuality, and compliance curation. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are compared with the existing human markup. MIMR is additionally compared with blinded human judgments on a 10% webpage sample evaluated by 7 participants.

value: [Experimental result] Factuality agent: intrinsic precision 0.866, recall 0.938, F1 0.901; extrinsic precision, recall, and F1 all 0.945.
[Experimental result] Compliance agent: precision 0.900, recall 0.914, F1 0.907.

[Experimental result] Across 180 webpages, human markup had 5690 input triples, 4875 valid, 3315 factual, and 2719 compliant; rejection rate 52.2%. GPT-3.5 had 4190 input, 3369 valid, 2489 factual, and 2055 compliant; rejection rate 50.9%. GPT-4 had 5260 input, 4613 valid, 3573 factual, and 3113 compliant; rejection rate 40.8%.
[Experimental result] Aggregate MIMR scores were human 0.687 and GPT-3.5 0.585, while GPT-4 scored 0.707 against human 0.568.
[Experimental result] MIMR agreement with blinded human preferences was substantial: Cohen’s Kappa 0.750 for GPT-3.5 and 0.895 for GPT-4.
[Author interpretation] GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 help improve webpages in low and medium quantiles, whereas humans perform better in the highest instance/property quantiles.

value: [Author claim] The pipeline evaluates real webpages with a large Schema.org ontology rather than only short benchmark sentences and small schemas.
[Author claim] It provides separate validity, factuality, and compliance curation stages and evaluates the two LLM-based agents independently.
[Experimental result] GPT-4 achieved a higher aggregate MIMR than human markup after curation, and MIMR showed substantial agreement with blinded human judgments.

[Review-level inference] The use of visible webpage text and ontology documentation creates a practical ground-truth-free evaluation design for open-ended markup generation, although it does not remove evaluator error.

value: [Author-reported weakness] The MIMR metric is coarse-grained and purely quantitative; a markup with fewer but more important properties may be qualitatively better.
[Experimental limitation] Triple-level factuality and compliance checks can generate false positives and false negatives because they omit broader context.
[Experimental finding] The agents make false-positive and false-negative errors, including failures with implicit meanings, negation, ambiguous properties, and external links.
[Review-level inference] Aggregate MIMR is not a direct measure of semantic correctness or downstream knowledge-graph utility because it measures contribution to a merged markup.
